Poland is investing billions in a major military build-up to deter Russia, strengthen NATO and bolster European security. Photo by WOJTEK RADWANSKI / AFP via Getty Images Article content Poland, with an imminent high-priced military ramp-up, is betting that the cost of peace is cheaper than the price of war with Russia. Sign In or Create an Account or View more offers Article content In a watershed defence spend, coming from a European Union loan, Warsaw is pouring nearly 44 billion euros ($71 billion) into stepping up its military infrastructure. Why now? That’s obvious for anyone following Moscow’s unyielding provocations. Article content Article content Article content Jets scrambling to intercept Russian aircraft over the Baltic, cyberattacks on Polish railways and hospitals, and drones and missiles straying across its borders have all convinced Poland’s political class that deterrence can’t be put off for an indeterminate future budget cycle. Article content With the new loan, Poland’s the largest single beneficiary of Security Action for Europe’s (SAFE) 150‑billion-euro defence budget. The loans are earmarked for modernizing the military, expanding the domestic arms sector, and rewarding Polish firms that collaborate with defence manufacturers. Government plans plot roughly 4.8 per cent of the nation’s GDP going to defence. Article content “This is a watershed moment in the history of both Poland and the European Union,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk said May 8 in Warsaw, at a ceremony for the signing of the agreement, AFP reported . “Poland will be safer in these difficult and highly risky times.” Article content Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk arrives for a dinner of the Coalition of the Willing to support Ukraine at the French presidential palace in Paris in July. Photo by LUDOVIC MARIN / AFP via Getty Images Article content According to Dominic Roszak, president of the Canadian Polish Congress, and Stakeholder Relations Lead for the 2023 Warsaw Security Forum, “Poland has long warned the rest of Europe of Russia’s expansionist ambitions, even when other EU leaders weren’t always willing to listen.” Article content Article content He continued: “Poland sees itself as a guarantor of regional security along the EU and NATO’s eastern frontier, including the more vulnerable Baltic states. I share the view that a strong and effective military is the only way to deter Russia from a direct confrontation with NATO.” Article content Read More Canadians support sending troops to Poland if Russia invades: poll Adam Zivo: By sending drones into Poland, Putin is taunting the West Advertisement 1 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Poland’s history with Nazi and Communist occupations has made his countrymen “wary of being caught unprepared for foreign aggression,” he said. Article content Even though there were “public political disputes” over where the loan should come from — be it domestic financing or SAFE — he insists now there is “a broad consensus across government institutions and the mainstream political spectrum that, whatever the mechanism, a rapid defence build-up is necessary.” Article content The Polish military industry upgrade has won admirers here in Canada. According to Breaking Defense, Ottawa is poised to purchase Polish drones. A statement from the Canadian Department of National Defence said the two countries intended to pursue “joint projects involving emerging technologies.” Moreover, Poland was the featured country at CANSEC (Canada’s Global Defence & Security Trade Show) in Ottawa this spring, and Canada will be the lead nation at the MSPO defence expo in Kielce this September. Article content “With both countries (Canada and Poland) now participating in SAFE and deepening their strategic bilateral cooperation, this stops being a purely national spending story, and has the potential to become a shared industrial base. For defence manufacturers on both sides of the Atlantic, that is the opportunity of the decade,” Roszak said. Article content A Polish soldier launches an interception drone of the American MEROPS counter-drone system during tests at the Nowa Deba military training ground, south-eastern Poland, on November 18, 2025. Photo by WOJTEK RADWANSKI / AFP via Getty Images Article content There are a few potential downsides to Warsaw’s new plan – none of which are, in Roszak’s view, qualitatively or quantitatively much to worry about. Article content “The risk I would actually put at the top of the list is procurement delay. Poland’s planning anticipates the possibility of a confrontation with Russia within even the next five years, and there are still capability gaps to fill. Poland is determined to close them quickly, and has supercharged its procurement efforts, creating a dedicated role to drive the effort.” By the end of May, he added, Poland’s defence minister had already confirmed the signing of 50 contracts under SAFE, with a value close to 120 billion zloty, or over half of Poland’s total allocation. Article content There is a risk, he conceded, of Russia pre-emptively moving towards escalation, ahead of Poland’s military readiness. But he also said: “NATO’s resolve is the single biggest deterrent to a westward expansion of the current conflict. Poland led the way at the start of the full-scale (Russian) invasion of Ukraine by supplying weaponry to the Ukrainians, that some said would lead to ‘escalation.’” Article content Article content A key indicator of the program’s success “will be a strong and sovereign Ukraine, because stability to Poland’s east is inseparable from Poland’s own.” Article content Katarzyna Lesperance, a native-born Pole and owner of the Starka distillery in Szczecin, Poland, comes from a family of military — first her father, and then her brother, a former senior-level official in the ministry of defence. “People are afraid,” she said, of a potential conflagration. Article content Katarzyna, who studied naval academics at the Heroes of Westerplatte Polish Naval Academy in Gdynia, said that “most people are for the military” build-up. Russia, she added, “would be so crazy to invade right now,” but continues “a lot of provocation.” Article content Katarzyna lives with her husband David Lesperance, of Lesperance & Associates, and 12-year-old twins, in Gdynia, a port city on the Baltic, where intense early fighting of the Second World War began. Their apartment overlooks the port where naval vessels come out, and container ships bring in military hardware. There’s a military airfield in the city, with frequent flybys. Article content Article content Their apartment’s about two-and-a-half hours from the Belarusian border, and Kaliningrad, Russian territory, Lesperance said. Article content Poles today “are conscious of bad things happening. It’s a part of Polish history…. So they are attuned to kind of, better be prepared, and prepare for the worst, hope for the best, and work for the best,” he said. His sense is that “reliance on America for monies and/or sophisticated systems, which need constant replacement and upgrading” is believed to be precarious and unpredictable, “with (U.S. President) Donald Trump being Donald Trump.” Article content A former diplomat echoed that Poland’s military surge is meant to avoid a far costlier, bloodier war. Article content “For us, safety — or I would say lack of safety — is a very present topic. It started long before the full state invasion of Russia to Ukraine,” said Natalia Walsh Iwaszko, formerly vice consul economic affairs, at the Consulate General of the Republic of Poland in Toronto. “Russia has been always a threat for centuries…. And we know that there is not much needed for Russia to be encouraged to attack again, either us or Baltic states.” Article content Born and raised in Poland, she is currently residing in Vancouver for a brief time, and writes for Defence24, Polish-based defence and security news. Article content To the argument that perceived brinkmanship might spur Moscow to fire first, before Poland has its full defensive walls up, she said such talk is “mostly created by Russian propaganda.” Article content Minister Bartosz Grodecki, head of the National Security Bureau of the Republic of Poland told the Post that in the nearly 30 years in NATO, his country has “transformed from a recipient of security to a creator of it” and that it has a “clear understanding of the goals and strategy of our main adversary — Russia — which is why, both domestically and internationally, we emphasize the importance of being able to defend against its imperialist ambitions.” Article content He added that the country is aware that in “the event of an attack, the costs of a defensive operation and the consequences of wartime destruction will be far greater than those incurred in building a resilient defence system.” Article content Our website is the place for the latest breaking news, exclusive scoops, longreads and provocative commentary. Add The New York Post on Google More than a quarter of sexual assaults involving US troops deployed overseas last year took place in Poland — a growing hub of the nation’s security posture in Europe, jarring new military data reveal. Reported assaults in Poland hit 73 last year as the US added 10,000 troops to bolster NATO’s eastern flank from the neighboring war in Ukraine and where new bases are under consideration, according to the data — which also show sexual assaults among US servicemembers down slightly worldwide by about 2%. The data comes from an annual report on sexual reports in the military required by Congress. A new Department of War report finds an overall decrease in sexual assault involving troops, and that more than a quarter of those assaults involving troops abroad were reported in Poland. Getty Images The number of sex assaults in Poland is twice as many as any other country where US troops are deployed, and it’s the third year it has led all nations, Task and Purpose reported . There are currently three times as many US troops in Germany as there are in Poland, with about 35,000 stationed there. The country has seen a rapid expansion of US forces, and has had some close calls with Russian drone and missile attacks on Ukraine. In just one incident in Poland, Army Sgt. Ulrich Kameni, a petroleum supply specialist, pleaded guilty in June to assaulting two women and maltreatment of another. He was sentenced to three years in prison after a military court martial at Camp Kosciuskzko. In a 2023 incident, Kameni berated and physically assaulted a female soldier under his supervision after she rebuffed his romantic advances, according to Army prosecutors. There was an earlier incident with a female soldier in Georgia. Then in 2024, while at a bar in Zielona Gora, Poland, a “highly intoxicated” Kameni began flirting with a Polish civilian. Later that night, when the two were alone, Kameni became aggressive and grabbed the woman by the neck, injuring her, prosecutors said. Congress requires annual reporting on sexual assault in the military. AFP via Getty Images Across the entire War Department, including those serving at home, there were 7,998 reports of sexual assault involving troops, down 2% from 8,196 in fiscal 2024. There was enough evidence to take disciplinary action against 1,321 individuals investigated for sexual assault, according to the report, which also drew on a worldwide Department of War survey. The real number of assaults is believed to be higher. About a third of those who said they experienced unwanted sexual contact reported it, according to survey results. Poland isn’t the only overseas location reporting significant numbers of sexual assaults involving US troops. Kuwait and Qatar, where military bases have been under repeated fire from Iran, also ranked among the countries with higher tallies, the data show. Out of 246 reported sexual assaults involving deployed troops, there were 30 in Kuwait, 24 in Qatar, 23 in Iraq, and 20 in Romania. The figures track where the assaults are reported. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) , who has pushed on the issue for years, said the overall decline in reported assaults was encouraging, adding that the numbers “appears to show meaningful movement in the right direction.” A US Army spokesman said its “firmly committed to eliminating sexual assault and sexual harassment from our ranks.” “This year’s report demonstrates meaningful progress across prevention, and survivor support,” said Maj. Travis Shaw without responding to questions about Poland. “Our goal is to ensure every soldier who experiences this crime feels safe coming forward to receive care and to hold offenders accountable. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm86.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Flames and smoke rise from an area struck by an air strike in Kandahar on Thursday By Tinshui Yeung Published 2 hours ago Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides. The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city. Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives". It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September. In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to. Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces. In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties. In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight. "People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed." Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians". Image source, EPA Image caption, A Taliban security official inspects the scene of Pakistani air strikes in Khost Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military". Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan". The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP. A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) , which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack. Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem. Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants. Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed. Image source, Kunar Police Office Image caption, An attack in Afghanistan's Kunar province has killed at least three civilians, according to the UN Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day. Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026. The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed , external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure". The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution. During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".
